problem: Existing social navigation methods either ignore social and environment context (human-model-based DRL, imitation learning) or use large VLMs that respond too slowly (about 0.6Hz) for dynamic humans. Neither adapts online to new social scenarios, and prior lifelong learning methods only cover human-model-based pipelines.
motivation: Service robots in hospitals, offices and care homes must respect personal space and social norms in scenarios not seen in training. Large VLMs have strong social reasoning but are too slow for real-time control, while lightweight models are fast but lack social understanding. Distilling the VLM's social reasoning into small encoders that can be updated online could give both speed and adaptability.
key_idea: Distill a large VLM's social-context captions into lightweight CLIP-style image and text encoders (SC-CLIP), use their embeddings for trajectory planning and selection, and keep updating the encoders online with VLM-labeled images.
insight: Each embedding contributes to trajectory quality. In the ablation on a MuSoHu hold-out set, removing E_I raised MSE from 0.2981 to 0.4412, removing E_T to 0.3838, and removing E_L to 0.4382 (before LLU update). The online LLU update improved every variant, for example full model MSE 0.2981 to 0.2521. Using the lightweight encoder at about 5Hz instead of querying GPT-4o at 0.6Hz is credited for the lower personal space violation duration. Caveat: the real-world comparison uses only 3 trials per scenario.
method: SC-CLIP distillation: GPT-4o generates a long and a short caption for 20k MuSoHu images (social scenario, objects and people, high-level navigation action). A ViT-L/14 image encoder and a transformer text encoder are trained Long-CLIP style, with a principal-component-extraction loss on the short caption (Eq. 3).

Lifelong Learning Updater: buffers a batch of |B|=50 RGB images during navigation, labels them with GPT-4, and fine-tunes both encoders with a symmetric image-text contrastive loss (Eq. 4). The text embedding database D_T is regenerated with the updated text encoder.

Trajectory Planning Network: a voxel LiDAR encoder (5 residual blocks), a goal FFN and the SC-CLIP image embedding are fused by 3 sequential cross-attention layers with 32 heads. A GRU head outputs K=5 trajectories, trained with winner-takes-all loss on MuSoHu expert trajectories.

Trajectory Selection Module: retrieves the text embedding from D_T by cosine similarity with the image embedding. It combines this with a GRU embedding of the candidate trajectories and picks the one matching the encoded high-level action, trained with cross-entropy (Eq. 7).
Navigation Controller: a PID controller converts the selected trajectory into linear and angular velocities (v, ω).

setting.backbone: SC-CLIP (ViT-L/14 image encoder + transformer text encoder, distilled from GPT-4o and updated online with GPT-4 labels), plus a trained TPN and TSM
setting.training_data: MuSoHu-based: 20,000 RGB images with GPT-4o long and short captions (SC-CLIP), 5,000 expert trajectories with LiDAR and RGB (TPN), 20,000 predicted trajectories with indices (TSM)
setting.observation: monocular RGB camera + 3D LiDAR point cloud + goal pose
setting.action_space: predicted 5 candidate trajectories of 10 future poses; PID converts the selected one to continuous linear/angular velocity

numbers.extra: 3 trials per scenario; Clearpath Jackal; ground truth is a teleoperated trajectory

numbers_note: No standard VLN or ObjectNav benchmarks. Results are on the authors' own real-world scenarios and a MuSoHu hold-out set. Table I reports one value per scenario without per-trial variance.
results: OLiVia-Nav had the lowest MSE, Hausdorff loss and PSV in all four real-world scenarios against VLM-Social-Nav (GPT-4o) and MultiSoc (DRL). For example, in the blind corner, MSE was 0.0236 vs 0.0755 and 0.1021, and PSV was 0.4 s vs 2.6 s and 2.8 s. The one exception in the table is static groups + dynamic people, where MultiSoc's MSE (0.2747) is higher but close. The differences were statistically significant (Friedman p<0.001; Wilcoxon p<0.025).
limitations: Evaluated in only four scenarios with 3 trials each in one building, with a teleoperated ground truth from a single researcher, and no large crowds (left as future work).
The lifelong update depends on querying a large VLM (GPT-4) for labels, and only one update iteration is evaluated; catastrophic forgetting is not analyzed.
Metrics measure similarity to a single expert trajectory and PSV, not success rate or collision rate.
